Most people push really hard for 401k contribution on account of the outdated premise that "free money" trumps all. The problem is in part what you stated, that you could lose those savings in what you'll pay in interest.

The other issue occurs when you're young and more likely to switch companies every year or two. Most vesting schedules require you to stay at 5-7 years to obtain the full amount of your free money. Anything less than that, and you'll usually get short-changed. So that "free money" isn't yours for a significant period of time, and if you don't plan on staying for that long with your current employer, the match becomes less enticing

Great points;

I'd also like to add that Roth IRAs (and traditional IRAs to a lesser degree) are more attractive that 401ks in a lot of ways. 401ks you pay tax on disbursement, IRAs contributions are post tax. With IRAs you're generally taxed less because you're taxed when you're younger (and presumably in a lower tax bracket than when you're older).

Great points! How you allocate your investments across each type of account depends on your stage of life in order to minimize taxation and maximize returns. It also depends on when you want to retire. Those who want to retire early will have different needs than the majority of us planning to retire at 70

My basic algorithm

  • 401k = Invest base salary % into whatever the limit is for employer match for 401k (don't invest more)

  • Individual Investment In Stocks = 100 - my age (ex: if I'm 30 have 70% of my investments in stocks, or stock based etfs, etc.)

  • Roth IRA = Put max for my income tax bracket.

  • Emergency Fund = 2 Months living expenses (based on how long it takes to find another job in my industry. Between the public health exchanges and renters insurance I feel pretty protected in case of emergency, 3-6 months seems excessive to me.)

I should also note that I don't have any debt (outside of mortgage payments).

My company does not match at all so I was wondering if it's better (and if can) open my own 401k somewhere else because the funds my company offers as options aren't my first choices.

I read also that you can designate a 401k to be a Roth? Can I do that if I already have a Roth IRA?

It sounds like you might want to just do it yourself with a Traditional IRA. The difference between a Traditional IRA and a 401k isn't really about you (the contributor). 401k Plans give tax breaks to corporations that use them (for non profits / government it's 457 plans), Traditional IRAs do not give tax breaks which is why corporations offer 401ks. When you leave your job you can roll your old 401k into a Traditional IRA (essentially the old corporation no longer gets tax breaks because you don't work there anymore and no one is making contributions).

If your company doesn't match in their 401k there's no reason to use it over opening your own Traditional IRA account AFAIK. The advantage to your own IRA account is you get to choose the brokerage and have greater freedom over the set of investments.
